newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler, UAW set to resume formal talks Modnay.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler, UAW set to resume formal talks Modnay.

text.p: Union and Chrysler Corp. bargainers were scheduled to resume formal talks Monday to end a crippling parts plant strike, even though a union official said Sunday that neither side has shown any sign of softening its position.
Despite a "cooling off" period, United Auto Workers Local 51 President Sam Nardicchio said informal communications over the last few days have gone nowhere.
"We're dug into our position. We're not going anywhere," he said.

About 1,800 members of Local 51 struck Chrysler's Mound Road engine plant in Detroit early Thursday, April 10. Workers are demanding that Chrysler drop its plans to shift production of drive shafts from the plant to an outside supplier, a move that could cost the local 250 jobs.

The walkout forced Chrysler to suspend production Friday at four pickup truck, sport/utility and full-size van assembly plants. The facilities are located in Detroit and nearby Warren, Mich., St. Louis and Windsor, Ontario. About 12,080 workers were idled by the move.
The Mound Road plant is the only one that supplies the V-6, V-8 and V-10 truck engines Chrysler uses in its Dodge Ram and Dakota pickup trucks, Jeep Grand Cherokee sport/utilities and full-size vans.
Chrysler spokesman Tony Cervone said Sunday that other than some individual shift adjustments, the company does not plan to idle any more plants as a result of the walkout.
"We don't expect to bring any more plants down completely," he said.

Analysts have estimated a prolonged strike could cost the automaker about $70 million a week in lost profits. About two- thirds of Chrysler's U.S. sales come from light truck products - - pickups, minivans and sport/utilities -- and the Ram pickup and Grand Cherokee are some of its most profitable vehicles.

Union members, already angry over the outsourcing plans, were infuriated by Chrysler's disclosure Friday that Chairman Robert Eaton took home $12.6 million from compensation and stock options last year.
Eaton told WWJ-Radio during a reception for Detroit's new Museum of African American History Friday night that he does not expect the walkout to last long.
Meanwhile, General Motors Corp. and UAW Local 1999 were scheduled to hold talks Sunday to end a nine-day walkout by 3,500 workers at GM's Oklahoma City, Okla., car plant.
A union member who declined to give his name said Sunday that UAW members do not expect a quick settlement in that strike.
"We're looking at the first of the month, unless they want the cars," he said.
The plant is the main source of the new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass. The redesigned mid-size sedans are an important part of GM's efforts to regain marketshare in the mid-size segment.
